\chapter{Grande --- the First Word for What a Thing Is Like}
\label{ch:grande}
\hlchaptermodality{58}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can describe a thing with an adjective after the noun.}

I can describe a thing with an adjective after the noun.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[grande]{grande}

\label{lesson:ES-C09-grande}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}she is.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Es}.) You can say who someone \textbf{is} and what they \textbf{do}.

You still cannot say what anything is \textbf{like}. That starts here.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{grande}} — big
\end{quote}

Latin \textbf{grandis} meant \emph{full-grown}. English took it whole and never changed it: a \textbf{grand} piano is the big one, a \textbf{grandiose} plan is oversized, and a \textbf{grandmother} is — literally — the full-grown mother.

\begin{quote}
\emph{grande} $\leftarrow$ \emph{grandis} $\to$ \textbf{grand}, \textbf{grandiose}, \textbf{aggrandise}
\end{quote}

Say it: \emph{grande}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: where it goes, and what it does not do}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{A describing word usually comes \emph{after} the noun in Spanish.}
\end{quote}

English puts it in front — \emph{a big house}. Spanish puts it behind:

\begin{quote}
\emph{una casa \textbf{grande}} — a big house
\end{quote}

And \emph{grande} does not change for a man or a woman:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{el libro grande} & the big book \\
\emph{la casa grande} & the big house \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You have met that already. \emph{Estudiante} and \emph{artista} do not shift either. Some Spanish words agree with gender and some simply do not, and the ending tells you which: \emph{-o/-a} words like \emph{bueno/buena} shift, \emph{-e} words like \emph{grande} sit still.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{una casa grande}
  \item \emph{el libro grande}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does a describing word go? (\textbf{After} the noun.)

And which endings sit still? (\textbf{-e} ones, like \emph{grande}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
